new_statements.quote: Diraytata has two tones: high and low. The high tone is represented by ( ´ ) and the low tone is unmarked. In monosyllabic words with CVC pattern, the vowel always carry a high tone [...] On the other hand monosyllabic words with CVVC or CVCC pattern carry a low tone [...] Most of the disyllabic words receive a high tone in their initial syllable [...] However, there are a few disyllabic words which have a high tone in their ultimate syllable [...] In trisyllabic words the ultimate syllable receives the high tone [...] We can say that Diraytata is a tone-accent language as there is a single high tone in a word.
new_statements.citation: Wondwosen Tesfaye Abire. 2006. Aspects of Diraytata Morphology and Syntax: A Lexical-Functional Grammar Approach. Doctoral thesis, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Trondheim. 266 pp. hdl:11250/243978
new_statements.locator: Ch. 1, sec. 1.7.3 'Accentual patterns', pp. 11-12 (PDF pp. 27-28), incl. footnote 1 on p. 12
new_statements.rule_in_words: One culminative high tone (accent) per word; the author calls Diraytata a 'tone-accent language'. Placement by shape: CVC monosyllables carry H (káp 'mouth', tór 'spear'); heavy CVVC/CVCC monosyllables have no H (paas 'cleaver', arp 'elephant'); most disyllables have H on the initial syllable (sóha 'meat', hópa 'sandals', rífant 'hair'), but a few have final H (harrét 'donkey', haayyá 'wind'); trisyllables have H on the final syllable (mat'aat'ét 'potato', torrayyá 'locust'). So the position is largely shape-conditioned but not fully predictable for disyllables (lexical residue). Footnote 1 (p. 12): 'Diraytata is a tone-accent language in that words carry a single high tone (cf. Hayward 1999:231)' -- note that the bibliography's Hayward 1999 entry is 'East Ometo verb paradigms', SOAS WPL 9: 301-316, so this citation looks garbled.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; a single high tone per word is asserted.
new_statements.exceptions: A few disyllabic words carry the high tone on the final rather than the initial syllable (harrét 'donkey', haayyá 'wind', paac'ét 'beard'); heavy monosyllables (CVVC, CVCC) are low-toned. The author states that pitch is not marked in the rest of the thesis as it is irrelevant to the morphosyntactic study.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms of (mostly) nouns elicited in isolation; south (Gidole highland) variety. Brief phonology notes (sec. 1.7) in a syntax thesis, not a dedicated prosodic study; no instrumental data. Related: Wondwosen 2020 (Macrolinguistics 8(2): 84) adds that word-final short vowels with low tone are deleted in Diraytata (citing Hayward 1981).
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is from Wondwosen Tesfaye's 2006 NTNU thesis, which is explicitly based on the south (highland) variety of Diraytata spoken in and around Gidole town (thesis p. 4; Black 1973a distinguishes west, east and south varieties). The other opened phonology, Tesfaye 2023 'Kussummiya phonology' (Glottolog files it under dira1242), describes Kussummiya/Afa Kussummiya of Gatto (Kusume people), which the article itself says is mutually intelligible with Konso and Mashooleya but only partly with Diraytata; it is silent on stress/tone and is not the basis of the statement.

sources.note: Sec. 1.7.3 'Accentual patterns' pp. 11-12: two tones H/L, single H per word ('tone-accent language'); CVC monosyllables H, CVVC/CVCC monosyllables L, most disyllables initial H (a few final), trisyllables final H; pitch not marked elsewhere in the thesis. The earlier scan could not retrieve this PDF (NTNU Open redirects to nva.sikt.no); it was obtained here through the NVA API filelink endpoint.

sources.note: The primary modern description of Dirayta nominal morphology by a Cushiticist who marks accent/tone in his transcriptions (ɗiraytá, ɗiráaŝ on the abstract page) and cites Leben on tone; it is the source Wondwosen 2006/2020 rely on for Dirayta tone facts and is the most likely place for an authoritative statement of the accent system.
